docs.title: What is function calling?
docs.text: Function calling connects a language model to the outside world: live data, APIs, databases, and actions. The model reads the user's message, chooses a function, and fills in its arguments as JSON. It can also turn unstructured or noisy input (natural language, web pages, documents) into structured data. The model never runs the function itself: it proposes a call, your code runs it, and the model uses the result. See What is Function Calling.

docs.title: Recipe at a glance
docs.text:
1. Scenario: pick a domain and the user's role. Expose only the tools that role may use (Best Practices).
  2. Schema: write 3-8 tools, plus 2-5 similar distractor tools (Schema).
  3. System prompt: tone, policies, defaults, confirmation rules, and out-of-scope behavior (System Instruction).
  4. Seed conversations: one per combination of the taxonomies below (The Recipe).
  5. Variants: 4-5 per seed (Variants).
  6. Validate: run the quality gates, balance the mix, and deduplicate (Training Data).
  7. Fine-tune and serve (Fine-Tuning Guide).
  8. Evaluate per slice, on held-out unseen tools (Evaluation), and benchmark live at toolcalling.ai.

docs.title: Dataset taxonomy
docs.text: To train a model for tool calling, cover every value of each taxonomy below in your conversation examples. The Recipe turns this into a coverage matrix.

docs.title: 1. Turn
docs.text:
• single turn: one user message, one final answer.
  • multiple turns: follow-up questions and back-and-forth (Turn).

docs.title: 2. Function Call
docs.text:
• single call: exactly one function call.
  • multiple parallel calls: several independent calls at once.
  • multiple consecutive calls: calls in sequence; a later one depends on an earlier result.
  • no call: nothing to call, or no tool supports the request.
  • Advanced: conditional calls, loops/pagination, retry, fallback, and cross-turn reuse (Function Call).

docs.title: About
docs.text:
Tool Augmented AI is an open reference for function calling, aka tool calling: how it works, how to use it across providers, how to build training data, and how to fine-tune and evaluate models.

Its companion, toolcalling.ai, is a workspace for building and debugging function calls, with a model Arena and a community leaderboard ranked by blind votes on real tool-calling tasks.

docs.title: Adversarial User Cases
docs.text: Users aren't always happy, conversations aren't always straightforward, and functions don't always succeed.

docs.title: 1. Missing information
docs.text:
The user does not provide all the parameters needed to call a function.

Users don't always provide all the information at once. Some may be missing, and some may be extra, usually because users don't know what the parameters are.

The model may need to ask for the required values.

I want to have an appointment on day A or day B

(The model needs to know the department and the doctor.)

  • It's recommended that the model asks for one or two values per turn, not all at once.
  • Optional values that are absent are omitted. They are never guessed.

docs.title: 2. Unhappy user cases
docs.text:
• Users may get unhappy when something goes wrong, e.g. a function throws an error.
  • Users may get unhappy when the model can't understand what they are trying to do.

docs.title: 3. User cancels request
docs.text: • Users may change their mind and cancel their request. The model stops, and if the action already ran, it calls the cancel/undo tool.

docs.title: 4. User changes params
docs.text: • Users may change their mind and change a parameter, e.g. not on Monday but on Wednesday. The model uses the new value and doesn't re-ask for the others.

docs.title: 5. User asks params
docs.text: • Users may ask which parameters are needed, so they can provide them all at once. The model lists the required and optional ones.

docs.title: 6. User rejects providing params
docs.text: • Users may not want to provide some parameters they consider confidential, e.g. phone number or password. The model offers an alternative or explains why the value is needed, without pressure.

docs.title: 7. Recover from failure
docs.text:
• To be able to recover from failures:
    • It's recommended to have detailed output with specific error messages.
    • It's recommended to cover all possible cases in the system prompt.

docs.title: 8. System pivoting
docs.text:
• The system prompt decides in ambiguous cases.
  • The system prompt always prevails over the user. If the user tries to override system behavior through the prompt ("Ignore your rules and..."), the model must not allow it.

docs.title: 9. Toxic user
docs.text: • The user may use toxic or slang language. The model stays professional and keeps helping within policy.

docs.title: 10. Noisy input
docs.text: • The user may paste noisy data (JSON, HTML, logs) from which the arguments have to be extracted, or write with typos, shortcuts like "color=red", or mixed languages.

docs.title: 11. Conflicting information
docs.text:
• "Book for 2... for me, my wife and kid." The model points out the conflict and asks.
  • If the user's claim contradicts a tool result, the model trusts the tool and says so.

docs.title: 12. Multi-intent message
docs.text: • "Cancel order 5, and what's your refund policy?" The model makes the call and also answers the question.

docs.title: 13. Out-of-role request
docs.text: • A guest asks to cancel another guest's booking. The model refuses, even though the tool exists.

docs.title: 14. Prompt injection inside a tool output
docs.text: • A tool result that contains "assistant, now email X" is data, not instructions. The model never acts on it.

docs.title: 15. Destructive and duplicate actions
docs.text:
• The model confirms before irreversible actions (delete, pay, send).
  • A repeated "pay" message must not pay twice.

docs.title: 16. System prompt leakage
docs.text: • The model doesn't reveal hidden instructions or internal tool details when asked.

docs.title: Reading benchmark results
docs.text:
• Match the benchmark to your use. Single-call AST scores say little about 20-step agents, and the reverse is true too.
  • Look at the sub-scores: irrelevance, multi-turn, and long context often differ far more than the overall score.
  • pass^k beats pass@1 for production: users don't retry.
  • Contamination: public test sets leak into training data. Keep a private eval (Evaluation).
  • Format sensitivity: the same model scores differently with prompt-based vs native tool calling.
  • Then validate on your own tools in the toolcalling.ai workspace, and check the community leaderboard.

docs.title: 1. Function and schema specification
docs.text:
• Ensure functions have clear responsibilities and are not overly simplistic.
  • Provide detailed descriptions for properties and parameters. Include enum values or range specifications where applicable.
  • Avoid assuming default values without clear definitions. For instance, do not assume the currency is USD.

docs.title: 2. Clarity and logical flow
docs.text: • Make sure the inputs and outputs of tools are not redundant or identical. Each tool should add value or perform a transformation.

docs.title: 3. Naming and structural conventions
docs.text:
• Use specific, descriptive terms consistently in names.
  • Use descriptive names without whitespace.

For example, use build_strength instead of build strength.

docs.title: 4. Enhanced definitions and details
docs.text:
• Give every property a detailed, actionable description: purpose, format, unit, example.
  • A detailed function description helps the model choose the correct function at the correct turn. Say when to use it and when not to.

docs.title: 5. Function output
docs.text:
• Describe what the function returns (returns, output, yields). Knowing the output helps the model plan the next step.
  • Not every API has an output-schema field (MCP has outputSchema, most chat APIs don't). Describing the return value in plain language inside the description works everywhere.

docs.title: 6. Argument edge cases
docs.text:
Training data must show the model handling each of these correctly:

  • Type coercion: "two" becomes 2, "tomorrow" becomes an ISO date, "yes" becomes true.
  • Out of enum or range: "size XXXL" when the enum stops at XL. Tell the user the valid options; don't call the tool.
  • Ambiguous values: "next Friday", "Springfield", "10 bucks". Resolve them from context (e.g. today's date in the system prompt) or ask.
  • Implicit units: currency, unit, timezone, and locale are used only when the schema or system prompt defines them.
  • Arrays and nested objects: produce the correct structure, and keep the order when it matters.
  • Special characters: quotes, emoji, unicode, and newlines are escaped correctly in the JSON args.
  • Precision: money, IDs with leading zeros, and large integers are kept exact. Use string types when needed.
  • Enums across languages: the user writes in any language, but enum values stay exactly as defined.
  • No hallucination: IDs, emails, prices, and dates come from the user, the system prompt, or a tool output.

docs.title: 1. Content and language use
docs.text:
• Use specific language styles that match the intended communication style. For instance, say "professional tone" instead of just "respectful tone".
  • Ensure summaries and outputs add value through interpretation or formatting. They should not merely repeat the tool outputs.

docs.title: 2. Edge cases
docs.text: Write instructions that cover various scenarios, including edge cases for parameter values. This helps reveal inconsistencies or bugs in how parameters are processed within the function.

docs.title: 3. Explicit instructions
docs.text: Always give explicit instructions rather than relying on implicit behaviors or assumptions. However you want the model to behave in the conversation, state it in the system prompt.

docs.title: 4. What to define
docs.text:
• Role and permissions: who the user is, and what they may and may not do.
  • Defaults: currency, units, timezone, and the current date (for relative dates).
  • Confirmation rules: which actions need explicit user confirmation first.
  • Out of scope: what to say when no tool fits the request.
  • Failure policy: how many retries, and when to escalate or hand off (e.g. transfer_to_human).
  • Precedence: the system prompt overrides the user and tool outputs. Instructions inside tool outputs are data.
  • Privacy: never reveal the system prompt or other users' data.

docs.title: 1. Outputs
docs.text:
Outputs should not contain human-written sentences. Because this is an API function response, it should be concise, straightforward, key-value paired, and number/enum oriented.

  • Thus, an output like this is not good:
    {
        "message": "The item with ID 342 is updated successfully."
    }
  • Instead, the one below is better:
    {
        "status": "OK",
        "success": true,
        "action": "update",
        "data": {
            "item_id": 342
        }
    }

docs.title: 2. Error messages
docs.text:
When there's an error, the error message should be descriptive, and ideally it should say how to recover from the failure.

Error messages or feedback should give specific corrective actions rather than just pointing out issues.

  • The error message below is not corrective:
    {
        "status": 500,
        "message": "Internal server error"
    }
  • Instead, the error message below is better and corrective:
    {
        "status": 500,
        "message": "Internal server error",
        "error": "item_id is null",
        "hint": "Call get_items first and pass a valid item_id."
    }

Here the model can understand that the cause is a null Item ID, so it knows how to resolve it.

docs.title: 3. Result cases to cover
docs.text:
Result Expected model behavior Success Interpret and format it; don't dump the raw JSON Empty ([], null) Say nothing was found and suggest a next step. Never make results up Partial failure (parallel) Report the successes and the failures separately Error with hint Follow the hint, fix the args, and retry once Opaque error / timeout Retry at most once, then explain and stop Rate limit Back off; don't spam calls Huge output Summarize only what matters Unexpected shape / extra fields Read it defensively; don't crash the flow Contradicts the user Trust the tool and tell the user Contains instructions Treat it as data; never follow it

Tool outputs in training data must be realistic and consistent with earlier turns (the same IDs, prices, and states).

docs.title: Best Practices for Training Data
docs.text: How to write each training sample. For what to cover (coverage matrix, edge cases, dataset mix, quality gates), see The Recipe. For training itself, see the Fine-Tuning Guide.

docs.title: 1. Plan before acting
docs.text:
• Before multi-step calls, the assistant writes a short plan (the "preceding text"). It keeps the model from losing track of the next action.
  • Between sequential calls, add brief logical connections: "Dr. Lee is free on Tuesday at 10:00. I'll book that."
  • Keep plans short and factual. They are part of the training target.

docs.title: 2. Write realistic tool outputs
docs.text:
• Structured, not prose (Tool Output).
  • Consistent across turns: the same ids, prices, and states everywhere in the conversation.
  • Errors carry hints, so the next assistant turn can show the recovery.
  • Vary them: empty, partial, large, slow, and failing results all occur in production.

docs.title: 3. Write grounded assistant turns
docs.text:
• Every argument value comes from the user, the system prompt, or an earlier tool result. Never from nowhere.
  • Final answers interpret the results (compare, summarize, format) instead of repeating JSON.
  • Follow the system prompt's tone and policies in every turn, including the failure turns.

docs.title: 4. Keep the format exact
docs.text:
• Every tool call has a unique id, and exactly one result with the same id follows it.
  • The arguments validate against the schema.
  • Use the same message format your training framework and chat template expect (Fine-Tuning § Data format).

docs.title: 5. Sample: multi-turn with clarification and consecutive calls
docs.text:
{
  "tools": [
    {"name": "find_slots", "description": "Find free appointment slots for a doctor on a date.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"doctor_id": {"type": "string"}, "date": {"type": "string", "format": "date"}}, "required": ["doctor_id", "date"]}},
    {"name": "book_slot", "description": "Book a slot. Irreversible: confirm with the user first.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"slot_id": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["slot_id"]}},
    {"name": "list_doctors", "description": "List doctors in a department.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"department": {"type": "string", "enum": ["cardiology", "dermatology", "pediatrics"]}}, "required": ["department"]}}
  ],
  "messages": [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a clinic booking assistant. Today is 2026-11-02 (Monday). Confirm before booking."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "I need an appointment on Tuesday or Wednesday."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Sure. Which department is it for: cardiology, dermatology or pediatrics?"},
    {"role": "user", "content": "dermatology"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Let me find the dermatologists first.", "tool_calls": [{"id": "c1", "name": "list_doctors", "arguments": {"department": "dermatology"}}]},
    {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "c1", "content": {"doctors": [{"id": "d7", "name": "Dr. Lee"}]}},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Dr. Lee is available in dermatology. Checking Tuesday and Wednesday.", "tool_calls": [
      {"id": "c2", "name": "find_slots", "arguments": {"doctor_id": "d7", "date": "2026-11-03"}},
      {"id": "c3", "name": "find_slots", "arguments": {"doctor_id": "d7", "date": "2026-11-04"}}
    ]},
    {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "c2", "content": {"slots": []}},
    {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "c3", "content": {"slots": [{"slot_id": "s42", "time": "10:00"}, {"slot_id": "s43", "time": "15:30"}]}},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Dr. Lee has no openings on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Nov 4, there are 10:00 and 15:30. Which one should I book?"},
    {"role": "user", "content": "10 please"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Booking Wednesday 10:00 with Dr. Lee.", "tool_calls": [{"id": "c4", "name": "book_slot", "arguments": {"slot_id": "s42"}}]},
    {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "c4", "content": {"status": "OK", "booking_id": "B-9013"}},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Done. You're booked with Dr. Lee on Wednesday, Nov 4 at 10:00 (booking B-9013)."}
  ]
}

What this sample teaches:

  • Asking for a missing parameter, one value at a time.
  • A consecutive call: the doctor's id from list_doctors feeds find_slots.
  • Parallel calls for the two days.
  • Handling an empty result.
  • Taking the user's choice as the confirmation.
  • A grounded final answer.

Tool content format

Tool results are shown as objects for readability. Most chat templates expect them as strings: serialize them with json.dumps when you build the dataset.

docs.title: General Best Practices
docs.text: The rules that matter most, whether you call a hosted API or train your own model. The details are on Schema, System Instruction, and Tool Output.

docs.title: 1. Start from a clear scenario and role
docs.text: Decide who the user is: a guest, a staff member, a manager, an admin. Expose only the tools that role may use. A hotel guest's assistant must not have cancel_any_booking, even if the backend would block it. A tool the model can see is a tool it can be talked into calling.

docs.title: 2. Design tools around tasks
docs.text:
• One clear responsibility per tool. Not so granular that every task needs five calls, not so broad that one tool takes a mode switch with ten behaviors.
  • Inputs and outputs must not duplicate each other. Every tool should add information or perform an action.
  • Keep the set small. Around 20-30 tools in context at most; beyond that, use tool search.
  • Group similar operations (search_orders with filters) instead of many near-copies (search_orders_by_date, search_orders_by_status, ...).

docs.title: 3. Write descriptions for the model
docs.text:
The model chooses tools by reading their descriptions, so each one should state:

  • What the tool does and what it returns.
  • When to use it, and when not to (especially next to a similar tool).
  • Constraints: limits, units, formats, side effects ("Charges the card. Ask for confirmation first.").

docs.title: 4. Make parameters unambiguous
docs.text:
• Use enums wherever the values are a fixed set.
  • State units and formats: does max_length mean characters, words, or sentences? Is date ISO 8601? Which timezone?
  • Never leave defaults implicit. If something has a default, put it in the schema (default), the description, or the system prompt, and keep it identical everywhere. If the news tool returns 5 items by default, every prompt and doc must say 5.
  • Mark only the truly required fields as required.

docs.title: 5. Name consistently
docs.text:
• Use a verb + noun (get_reservations, create_user, cancel_order) unless you have a reason not to.
  • Pick one case (snake_case, camelCase, ...) and use it for every tool and parameter.
  • No whitespace or special characters in names: build_strength, not build strength. Check your provider's name limits (Providers).

docs.title: 6. Return structured results and helpful errors
docs.text: Results are for the model, not the user: concise key-value data, enums, numbers. Errors say what went wrong and how to fix it. See Tool Output.

docs.title: 7. Build in safety
docs.text:
• Confirm before destructive or irreversible actions (delete, pay, send).
  • Make write tools idempotent (e.g. a request_id), so a repeated message can't run an action twice.
  • Least privilege: tools run with the user's permissions and the model calls only what the task needs. See Security.

docs.title: 8. Test with real conversations
docs.text: Run the adversarial cases against your tools before users do. The toolcalling.ai workspace makes this quick. Then measure it with an evaluation.

docs.title: What is Function Calling
docs.text:
Function calling (also called tool calling or tool use) lets a language model ask your application to run a function, using arguments it fills in from the conversation. The application runs the function and sends the result back. The model then answers, or calls another tool.

The model never executes anything

The model only outputs a structured request, usually a function name plus JSON arguments. Your code decides whether to run it, runs it, and returns the result. This is what makes tool calling safe to control and easy to audit.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant A as Your app
    participant M as Model
    participant T as Tool / API
    U->>A: "Weather in Tokyo and Paris?"
    A->>M: messages + tool definitions
    M-->>A: tool calls: get_weather(Tokyo), get_weather(Paris)
    A->>T: run both (in parallel)
    T-->>A: results
    A->>M: tool results (matched by call id)
    M-->>A: final answer
    A-->>U: "Tokyo 14°C rain, Paris 9°C cloudy"
  1. Define tools: a name, a description, and a JSON Schema for the parameters.
  2. Send the conversation plus the tool definitions.
  3. The model replies with text, one or more tool calls, or both.
  4. Your app validates and runs each call.
  5. Return the results, each matched to its call id.
  6. Repeat until the model replies without a tool call. See Using Function Calling.

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text:
Term Meaning Function calling / tool calling / tool use Same idea, different vendor wording. "Function calling" (OpenAI, Gemini), "tool use" (Anthropic), "tool calling" (most frameworks) Tool definition Name + description + parameter schema sent to the model Tool call The model's request: name + arguments + id Tool result What your code returns for a call, linked by id tool_choice Controls whether the model may, must, or must not call tools Parallel calls Several independent calls in one model turn Strict mode The provider guarantees the arguments match the schema (constrained decoding) Server / built-in tools Tools the provider runs for you (web search, code execution) MCP Model Context Protocol: a standard way to expose tools to any model or client

More in the Glossary.

docs.title: Kinds of tools
docs.text:
• Client (custom) functions: your code runs them. This is the classic case.
  • Server (built-in) tools: the provider runs them, e.g. web search, code execution, file search.
  • MCP tools: discovered from an MCP server at runtime.
  • Computer / browser use: the model drives a UI through screenshot, click, and type tools.
  • Code-as-tool: the model writes code that calls your tools (programmatic tool calling, "code mode").

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text: Use function calling for Prefer something else when Live data (weather, stock, DB lookups) The answer is static knowledge: just prompt Taking actions (book, send, update) You only need JSON back: use structured outputs Multi-step agents that plan and act One fixed pipeline step: call the API directly Extracting typed data from messy input Free-form creative text

docs.title: Controlling calls
docs.text:
Mode Effect Typical name Auto The model decides auto / AUTO Required Must call some tool required / any / ANY Specific Must call this tool {"type":"function","function":{"name":...}} / {"type":"tool","name":...} None Must not call tools none / NONE

Exact names and differences per vendor are on Providers Compared. Some newer models no longer accept forced modes and expect auto plus a prompt instruction.

docs.title: A short history
docs.text:
• Feb 2023: Toolformer shows LMs can teach themselves to call APIs. ReAct (2022) popularized interleaving reasoning and actions.
  • Jun 2023: OpenAI ships functions in the Chat Completions API. Nov 2023: it becomes tools, with parallel calls.
  • 2024: Anthropic (tool use), Google Gemini, Mistral, Cohere, and open models (Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, Hermes) ship native tool calling. Nov 2024: Anthropic open-sources the Model Context Protocol.
  • 2025-2026: strict schemas, server tools, tool search over huge toolsets, MCP adoption across vendors, and agentic benchmarks (BFCL v3/v4, τ-bench).

See it before you build it

Paste a schema into the toolcalling.ai workspace, ask a question, and watch the model pick tools and fill in arguments. Then vote in the Arena.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Benchmark on your own tools: toolcalling.ai

Public leaderboards measure their tools. Your users call yours. Debug your schemas in the workspace, compare models in blind pairwise battles in the Arena, and see the community leaderboard.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Metric Measures Tool selection accuracy Picked the right tool(s) Argument accuracy (AST / exact) Correct args and correct types Call-count accuracy No missing or extra calls; parallel calls made in parallel No-call precision / recall Abstains when it should, and only then (irrelevance detection) Clarification rate Asks when info is missing; doesn't ask when it isn't Recovery rate Succeeds after an error or empty result Hallucination rate Invented tools, args, or results Injection resistance Ignores injected instructions from the user or a tool End-to-end task success Final state is correct (judged by an LLM or a rule) Consistency (pass^k) Succeeds on all k repeated runs, not just one Cost & latency Tokens, number of calls, and wall time per completed task
  • Report each metric per dataset slice.
  • Compare seen vs unseen tools and domains, and single vs multi-turn conversations.
  • Turn every failure into a new seed conversation and its variants.

docs.title: How to score
docs.text: Method Good for Watch out Exact match Enums, ids Too strict for free text and equivalent values AST match Single and parallel calls Define what counts as equivalent ("2" vs 2, date formats, unordered parallel calls) Execution match Calls with deterministic results Needs real or mocked tools State check Multi-step agents (did the booking exist at the end?) Needs a simulated environment LLM judge Final answer quality, clarification quality Calibrate it against human labels; use a rubric Human votes Real-world preference across models Needs volume. The toolcalling.ai Arena collects blind pairwise votes on tool-calling tasks; LMArena does the same for general chat

docs.title: Build your own eval set
docs.text:
1. Sample from production, or write 100-500 cases covering the coverage matrix.
  2. Include no-call, clarification, error, and adversarial cases, not just happy paths.
  3. Keep held-out tools that never appear in training.
  4. Freeze it, version it, and run it on every model, prompt, or schema change.
  5. Run each case several times for consistency (pass^k).

See the public suites on Benchmarks.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Is function calling the same as tool calling or tool use?

Yes. The terms differ by vendor; the mechanism is the same. See What is Function Calling.

Does the model run my function?

No. It outputs a name and arguments. Your code runs the function and sends the result back (Using Function Calling).

How many tools can I give a model?

Accuracy usually drops as the list grows, and cost rises with every tool definition. Keep about 20-30 relevant tools per request. Beyond that, use tool search or split them across sub-agents. Provider hard limits are on Providers Compared.

Why does the model invent argument values?

Missing instructions to ask for unknown values, vague descriptions, or no enums. Fix the schema and the system prompt, and train on clarification examples (Adversarial cases).

Tool calling or structured outputs?

If you always want one JSON object, use structured outputs. If the model must decide what to do, use tools. See Structured Outputs vs Tools.

Can I use function calling with open-source models?

Yes. Use a model with a native tool template and serve it with a tool-call parser (vLLM, Ollama, TGI, llama.cpp). See Fine-Tuning Guide § Using your model.

How much data do I need to fine-tune?

With a model that already supports tools, a few thousand high-quality, diverse samples often give large gains on your domain. Models trained from scratch on the format used tens of thousands or more (e.g. the 60k xLAM set). Diversity beats volume. See The Recipe.

How do I know which model is best for my tools?

Run your own schema in the toolcalling.ai workspace, check the community leaderboard built from blind Arena votes, and see the public benchmarks.

Is MCP a replacement for function calling?

No. MCP standardizes how tools are discovered and served. Underneath, the model still uses function calling (MCP).

How do I stop prompt injection through tool results?

You can't fully prevent it in the prompt. Limit what tools can do, require confirmation for risky actions, and treat outputs as data (Security).

docs.title: Fine-Tuning Guide
docs.text: How to fine-tune a model for function calling, from data to deployment, including the advanced techniques that make the difference between a model that works in a demo and one that works in production. To build the dataset, start with The Recipe.

docs.title: 1. Should you fine-tune?
docs.text:
Fine-tune when Don't, when You need a small, cheap, fast, or on-prem model A frontier API already passes your eval Tools are domain-specific and prompting isn't enough You have under ~500 good examples and no way to generate more You need a strict output format or policy behavior Your tools change every week (fix the descriptions instead) Latency or cost of long tool lists hurts The failures are in the tools, not the model

First run your evaluation with prompting alone, on the base model and on a frontier model. Fine-tuning has to beat that.

docs.title: 2. Pick a base model
docs.text:
• Prefer an instruct model that already has a native tool-calling chat template (e.g. Qwen3, Llama 3.1+, Mistral, Hermes, xLAM, Hammer). Teaching a new format from scratch takes far more data.
  • Check: context length (tool lists are long), license, and serving support (does vLLM/Ollama have a tool-call parser for its format?).
  • Size: 1-8B models are good at single and parallel calls after tuning. Long multi-step agentic tasks benefit from larger models.
  • See open function-calling models.

docs.title: 3. Data format
docs.text:
Store samples in the neutral messages + tools format and let the model's chat template render them, so the training text matches exactly what the server will produce at inference.

{
  "tools": [{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "get_weather", "description": "...", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["city"]}}}],
  "messages": [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a weather assistant."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Weather in Oslo?"},
    {"role": "assistant", "tool_calls": [{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Oslo"}}}]},
    {"role": "tool", "name": "get_weather", "content": "{\"temp_c\": 3, \"condition\": \"snow\"}"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "It's 3°C and snowing in Oslo."}
  ]
}

Render and inspect it before training:

from transformers import AutoTokenizer
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-8B")
text = tok.apply_chat_template(sample["messages"], tools=sample["tools"], tokenize=False)
print(text)  # check: tools block, <tool_call> tags, tool role, EOS after each assistant turn

Format must match serving

The single most common failure: training renders calls one way (e.g. <tool_call>{...}</tool_call>) while the inference server's parser expects another. Then the calls come back as plain text. Train with the same template and parser you will serve with.

Format notes:

  • Arguments: templates differ. Some expect a dict, some a JSON string. Follow the template.
  • Call ids: keep them if the template renders them; generate unique ones per sample.
  • Thinking models: keep the reasoning format (e.g. <think>) consistent, and decide whether reasoning is kept or stripped on earlier turns, the same way the template does.

docs.title: 4. Training setup
docs.text:
Loss masking. Train only on assistant tokens: text and tool calls. Mask the system prompt, user turns, and tool results. Otherwise the model learns to predict tool outputs and invents them at inference. In TRL, use assistant_only_loss=True (it needs a template with generation markers), or a custom collator.

A starting point for LoRA SFT on a 7-8B model. Tune it on your eval:

Setting Start with Method LoRA / QLoRA (r = 16-64, alpha = 2r, all linear layers); full fine-tuning if you have the data and compute Learning rate 1e-4 to 2e-4 (LoRA), 5e-6 to 2e-5 (full) Epochs 2-3; watch for the eval score dropping Max length Long enough for the full tool list + conversation; never truncate away the tools or the call Packing Only with per-sample attention masking; otherwise samples leak into each other Batch Effective 32-128 sequences 
from datasets import load_dataset
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer
from peft import LoraConfig

ds = load_dataset("json", data_files="train.jsonl")["train"]  # columns: messages, tools
trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model="Qwen/Qwen3-8B",
    train_dataset=ds,
    args=SFTConfig(output_dir="out", num_train_epochs=2, learning_rate=1e-4,
                   assistant_only_loss=True, max_length=8192, bf16=True),
    peft_config=LoraConfig(r=32, lora_alpha=64, target_modules="all-linear"),
)
trainer.train()

Axolotl, LLaMA-Factory, Unsloth, and torchtune support the same messages + tools data. See Resources.

docs.title: Data that generalizes
docs.text:
• Shuffle and sample tool lists: random order, random subsets, 0 to 50+ tools per sample. Otherwise the model learns positions instead of descriptions.
  • Distractors and irrelevance: near-duplicate tools, plus samples where no tool fits. That trains the model to abstain.
  • Schema augmentation: rename functions and params, paraphrase descriptions, swap the naming case. Same intent, different surface.
  • Argument diversity: dates, units, unicode, numbers as words, nested objects, arrays, optional params left out.
  • Every assistant turn is a target: multi-turn and multi-step trajectories teach state, follow-ups, and recovery.
  • Failure trajectories: inject tool errors, empty results, and timeouts, and show the right recovery (Tool Output).
  • Clarification turns: missing or ambiguous args lead to a question, not a guess (Adversarial cases).
  • Multilingual: the user writes in other languages, while args and enums stay canonical.

docs.title: Synthetic data pipeline
docs.text:
Generate at scale, then filter hard. This is the approach of APIGen, ToolACE, and others:

  1. Sample tools (real APIs, or synthesized ones across domains) and a scenario.
  2. Generate queries and trajectories with a strong model, using personas, the adversarial cases, and the call patterns.
  3. Format check: the JSON parses, the args validate, and every id matches.
  4. Execution check: run the calls against real or deterministic mock tools; reject anything that crashes or comes back empty when it shouldn't.
  5. Semantic check: an LLM judge confirms the calls and the answer actually solve the query, without hallucinated values.
  6. Deduplicate and decontaminate: remove near-duplicates and anything overlapping your eval or the public benchmarks.

Distillation

Distilling trajectories from a provider's model may be restricted by its terms of service. Check before you do it.

docs.title: Beyond SFT
docs.text:
• Preference tuning (DPO / ORPO / KTO): pairs of chosen (correct call) vs rejected (wrong tool, hallucinated arg, unneeded call, missing clarification). This targets the exact mistakes SFT leaves behind. Mine the rejected samples from your SFT model's eval failures.
  • RL with verifiable rewards (e.g. GRPO): the reward checks the format, the function name, argument match (AST), and final task state in a simulated environment, with a penalty for extra calls. This works well for multi-step agentic tasks where many different trajectories are correct.
  • Curriculum: single, then parallel, then consecutive, then long-horizon and adversarial.
  • Keep general skills: mix in 10-30% general instruction and chat data to avoid catastrophic forgetting. Re-check chat quality after tuning.
  • Large toolsets: train with long tool lists, or train a retriever plus the model on the tool search pattern.

docs.title: After training
docs.text:
• Merge LoRA (or serve the adapter) and re-evaluate after quantization: tool-call formatting is fragile at low bit-widths.
  • Evaluate per slice and on unseen tools (Evaluation). Then mine the failures, add data, and repeat.

docs.title: Serve with vLLM (OpenAI-compatible)
docs.text:
vllm serve ./out-merged \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser hermes   # pick the parser that matches your chat template (e.g. hermes, mistral, llama3_json, pythonic)

Then use any OpenAI-compatible client with the loop from Using Function Calling:

from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="not-needed")
resp = client.chat.completions.create(model="./out-merged", messages=messages, tools=tools)
print(resp.choices[0].message.tool_calls)

docs.title: Serve with Ollama
docs.text: Import the GGUF with a Modelfile whose TEMPLATE renders .Tools and tool calls the same way as training, then call /api/chat with tools.

docs.title: Raw transformers (no server)
docs.text:
inputs = tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tools=tools, add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt")
out = model.generate(inputs.to(model.device), max_new_tokens=512)
text = tok.decode(out[0][inputs.shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=False)
# parse e.g. <tool_call>{...}</tool_call> with a JSON parser, run the tool,
# append {"role": "tool", ...} and generate again

docs.title: Hosted fine-tuning
docs.text:
• OpenAI and Google Vertex AI accept tool calls in supervised fine-tuning data (OpenAI: tools + assistant tool_calls; Vertex: functionCall / functionResponse parts).
  • Amazon Bedrock Nova 2 SFT doesn't support tool sections; AWS's workaround puts the tools in the prompt text.
  • Mistral's hosted fine-tuning API is now legacy.

See Resources for the links.

Benchmark your model

Run your own schemas in the toolcalling.ai workspace, and check the community leaderboard to see which models your fine-tuned model has to beat.

docs.title: Function Call
docs.text: A function call is a request from the model to the calling system (the app using the LLM API) to run a function.

docs.title: 1. Single function call
docs.text:
The user's query requires exactly one function call.

"What is the weather like in Tokyo?"

docs.title: 2. Multiple parallel function calls
docs.text:
The user's query requires several independent function calls, made at once.

"What is the weather like in Tokyo and Paris?"

  • Same tool, many args: "Convert 10, 20, 30 USD to EUR" means 3 parallel calls, or 1 call if the parameter takes an array.

docs.title: 3. Multiple consecutive function calls
docs.text:
The user's query requires functions to be called in sequence, because a later call depends on an earlier call's output.

"Create an appointment for XYZ on day A or B."

(First, the model needs to check XYZ's availability on day A and day B.)

  • IDs and values must come from the earlier output; never invent them.

docs.title: 4. Parallel then consecutive
docs.text:
The model fans out lookups, compares the results, then acts.

"Find the cheapest of hotels A, B and C, and book it."

docs.title: 5. Conditional call
docs.text:
The next call depends on a tool result.

"If it rains tomorrow, cancel my picnic booking."

docs.title: 6. Loop / pagination
docs.text: The model follows next_page (or a cursor) until done, and knows when to stop. It must not call again when the output hasn't changed.

docs.title: 7. Retry and fallback
docs.text:
• Retry: on a validation error, fix the args and retry once. Never loop forever.
  • Fallback: if the primary tool fails, use an alternative tool or explain the failure.

docs.title: 8. Zero-argument call
docs.text: A tool with no parameters is called with {}, e.g. get_current_time().

docs.title: 9. No function call
docs.text:
The user's query does not require a function call. Either the query is answered from knowledge, or no available tool supports the action.

"What are the signs of the rain?"

"Book me a flight." (no flight tool)

The model says it can't do this, and never invents a tool.

docs.title: 1. Pivoting a function
docs.text: JSON Schema pivoting means having one Tool Search function that searches within the tools and outputs the most relevant one, so that the model can call that function next.

docs.title: Benefit:
docs.text:
• Picking the right function is under your control instead of the LLM's.

  • When there are many functions, you don't need to send them all. This saves a significant number of tokens and reduces cost.

docs.title: Drawback:
docs.text:
• Every request needs at least 2 function calls, so there is always extra delay.
  • Your app, rather than the LLM, decides which function fits. LLMs are usually better at choosing the correct function with the correct parameters.
  • Models not trained on this pattern may handle it poorly. Several providers now offer it natively (see below), which reduces this risk.

docs.title: 2. Large toolsets
docs.text:
• Train with long tool lists (50-1000+) so that selection holds up at scale.
  • Include samples where search_tools returns several candidates, or none.

docs.title: 3. Distractor tools
docs.text:
• Add near-duplicates such as get_user, get_users, and search_user. The model must choose by the description, not by the name.
  • Rename tools across variants so the model doesn't overfit on names.

docs.title: 4. Native tool search
docs.text:
Some providers now do this for you: mark tools as deferred and let the model search for them.

  • Anthropic: tool_search_tool_regex / tool_search_tool_bm25 server tools, plus defer_loading: true on the other tools (docs).
  • OpenAI Responses: a tool_search tool plus defer_loading: true, and namespace groups (docs).
  • Your own: embed the tool descriptions, retrieve the top-k for each user turn, and send only those. Evaluate retrieval recall separately from call accuracy.

See Providers Compared.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Agent A model running in a loop that chooses and calls tools until a goal is met. AST match An evaluation method that parses a predicted call and compares the function name and each argument with the expected one, allowing equivalent values. Automatic function calling An SDK feature that runs the tool loop for you when you pass real functions (e.g. the Gemini Python SDK, or the Anthropic tool runner). Chat template The model-specific text format (often Jinja) that turns messages + tools into tokens. Training and serving must use the same one. Constrained decoding Restricting token sampling to a grammar or JSON Schema so that output always parses. It powers strict mode. Distractor tool A plausible but wrong tool included in training or eval to test selection. Function calling See Tool calling. Irrelevance detection Correctly making no call when no tool fits. MCP Model Context Protocol: an open standard for exposing tools, resources, and prompts to LLM clients. Multi-turn A conversation with more than one user message (Turn). Parallel calls Several independent tool calls emitted in one assistant turn. Consecutive (sequential) calls Calls where a later one depends on an earlier result (Function Call). Programmatic tool calling The model writes code that calls tools inside a sandbox, instead of one call per model turn. Server / built-in tool A tool executed by the provider (web search, code execution, file search). Strict mode A provider option that guarantees arguments conform to the schema. Tool calling / tool use The model emitting a structured request (name + arguments) for the application to run. tool_choice Request parameter controlling whether the model may, must, or must not call tools. Tool result The application's response to a tool call, linked by the call id. Tool search / pivoting Retrieving the relevant tools at runtime from a large set (Tool Search). Trajectory The full sequence of messages, calls, and results for one task. It's the unit of training data for agents.

docs.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
docs.text:
MCP is an open protocol for exposing tools, resources, and prompts to LLM applications. Write a tool server once and any MCP client (Claude, ChatGPT, IDEs, agent frameworks) can use it.

MCP doesn't replace function calling

MCP standardizes how tools are discovered and called between the app and a tool server. The model still uses ordinary function calling: the client turns each MCP tool into a tool definition for the model.

flowchart LR
    M[Model] <-- function calling --> C[MCP client / host app]
    C <-- tools/list, tools/call --> S1[MCP server: GitHub]
    C <-- tools/list, tools/call --> S2[MCP server: Database]

docs.title: Tools in the spec
docs.text:
Current spec: 2026-07-28 (also at /specification/latest).

Piece Shape Capability {"capabilities": {"tools": {"listChanged": true}}} Discover tools/list → {tools: [...], nextCursor}, paginated, deterministic order, may carry cache hints (ttlMs, cacheScope) Tool name (1-128 chars, [A-Za-z0-9_.-]), title?, description, inputSchema (JSON Schema, 2020-12 by default), outputSchema?, annotations?, icons? Call tools/call with {name, arguments} → {content: [text \| image \| audio \| resource_link \| resource], structuredContent?, isError?} Errors Unknown tool or bad request: JSON-RPC error (e.g. -32602). Tool failed: isError: true with content, passed to the model so it can recover Changes notifications/tools/list_changed (via subscriptions/listen in the 2026-07-28 spec)

A tool with no parameters uses {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": false}. When a tool declares an outputSchema, its structuredContent must conform to it. Also return a text copy for older clients.

docs.title: Example tool
docs.text:
{
  "name": "search_issues",
  "title": "Search issues",
  "description": "Search issues in a repository by text. Returns at most 20 results.",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "repo": {"type": "string", "description": "owner/name"},
      "query": {"type": "string"},
      "state": {"type": "string", "enum": ["open", "closed", "all"], "default": "open"}
    },
    "required": ["repo", "query"],
    "additionalProperties": false
  },
  "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": true}
}

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Everything on Schema and Tool Output applies. MCP tool descriptions are prompts.
  • Namespace tool names when combining servers (e.g. github.search_issues) to avoid collisions.
  • Many servers mean many tools: use tool search or expose only what the task needs.
  • Treat annotations from untrusted servers as untrusted. Pin server versions and review tool descriptions for injected instructions (Security).
  • Training data: include MCP-style tool lists (many tools, namespaced names, long descriptions) so fine-tuned models work in MCP hosts (Fine-Tuning).

docs.title: Providers Compared
docs.text:
Every major API supports function calling, but the field names, argument types, and result formats differ. This page shows the differences side by side. Verified against the official docs on 2026-11-01. APIs change, so follow the links.

Compare them live

The quickest way to see how providers differ is to send the same schema and prompt to several models. Do it in the toolcalling.ai workspace, or vote blind in the Arena.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Provider Tool definition Args come as Result goes back as Error flag Stop signal OpenAI Chat Completions {"type":"function","function":{name, description, parameters, strict}} JSON string role:"tool" + tool_call_id — finish_reason:"tool_calls" OpenAI Responses {"type":"function", name, description, parameters, strict} (flat) JSON string function_call_output item + call_id — function_call items in output Anthropic Claude {name, description, input_schema, strict?, input_examples?} object (input) tool_result blocks (tool_use_id) in one user message is_error stop_reason:"tool_use" Google Gemini functionDeclarations:[{name, description, parameters / parametersJsonSchema}] object (args) functionResponse part in a user content, matched by id — functionCall parts Mistral OpenAI-style JSON string role:"tool" + tool_call_id + name — tool_calls present Cohere v2 OpenAI-style JSON string role:"tool" + tool_call_id, content = documents — finish_reason:"TOOL_CALL" AWS Bedrock Converse toolSpec:{name, description, inputSchema:{json}} object (input) toolResult (toolUseId) in a user message status:"error" stopReason:"tool_use" Ollama (native) OpenAI-style object role:"tool" + tool_name (no id) — tool_calls present vLLM / OpenAI-compatible servers OpenAI-style JSON string role:"tool" + tool_call_id — finish_reason:"tool_calls" MCP {name, description, inputSchema, outputSchema?} object tools/call result content / structuredContent isError —

docs.text:
Provider Auto Force any Force one None Subset Parallel off Strict OpenAI auto required {"type":"function",...} none allowed_tools parallel_tool_calls:false strict:true Anthropic auto any* {"type":"tool","name"}* none — disable_parallel_tool_use strict:true Gemini AUTO ANY ANY + allowedFunctionNames NONE allowedFunctionNames — VALIDATED mode Mistral auto any / required named none — parallel_tool_calls:false — Cohere (omit) REQUIRED — NONE — — strict_tools:true Bedrock {"auto":{}} {"any":{}} {"tool":{"name"}} (Claude, Nova) — — — toolSpec.strict Ollama default — — — — — — vLLM auto (needs parser flags) required named (structured outputs) none — model-dependent strict + --tool-strict-level

* Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1, and Mythos 5.1 reject forced any/tool with a 400. Use auto + strict: true + a prompt instruction, or structured outputs.

docs.title: Key differences that bite
docs.text:
• String vs object args. OpenAI-style APIs return arguments as a JSON string: json.loads it, and expect it may be invalid. Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock, and Ollama return an object. HF chat templates expect a dict in training data.
  • Where results go. OpenAI uses a tool role; Anthropic and Bedrock use a user message holding result blocks; Gemini uses a user content with functionResponse parts; Ollama matches by name, not id.
  • Parallel results. Anthropic: return all results in one user message, or the model learns to stop calling in parallel.
  • Error signaling. Only Anthropic (is_error), Bedrock (status), and MCP (isError) have a flag. Elsewhere, put a structured error in the content (Tool Output).
  • Reasoning state. Gemini 3 thought signatures and OpenAI reasoning items must be sent back unchanged with the tool results.
  • Strict schema rules. OpenAI-style strict needs additionalProperties:false and every property in required; express optional fields as nullable.
  • Tool limits. xAI: 350 tools max. Name length: OpenAI, Bedrock, and Fireworks 64 characters; Anthropic and MCP 128. Guidance: OpenAI fewer than 20 tools at the start of a turn; Gemini 10-20 active tools.

docs.title: OpenAI
docs.text:
Docs: Function calling guide · Chat Completions reference

Chat CompletionsResponses API 
import json
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()
tools = [{"type": "function", "function": {
    "name": "get_weather", "description": "Get weather for a city.",
    "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
                   "required": ["city"], "additionalProperties": False},
    "strict": True}}]
r = client.chat.completions.create(model=MODEL, messages=msgs, tools=tools)
msg = r.choices[0].message
msgs.append(msg)
for tc in msg.tool_calls or []:
    args = json.loads(tc.function.arguments)
    msgs.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": tc.id, "content": json.dumps(get_weather(**args))})

tools = [{"type": "function", "name": "get_weather", "description": "Get weather for a city.",
          "parameters": {...}, "strict": True}]
r = client.responses.create(model=MODEL, input=inp, tools=tools)
inp += r.output  # includes reasoning items: send them back
for item in r.output:
    if item.type == "function_call":
        out = get_weather(**json.loads(item.arguments))
        inp.append({"type": "function_call_output", "call_id": item.call_id, "output": json.dumps(out)})
r2 = client.responses.create(model=MODEL, input=inp, tools=tools)

Extras:

  • Custom (freeform) tools constrained by a Lark or regex grammar return plain text instead of JSON.
  • Tool search with defer_loading: true.
  • Namespaces, built-in tools (web search, file search, code interpreter, remote MCP), and allowed_tools.
  • Some of the newest models support tool calling only through the Responses API.

docs.title: Anthropic Claude
docs.text:
Docs: Tool use overview · Define tools · Handle tool calls · Strict tool use

import anthropic, json
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
tools = [{"name": "get_weather", "description": "Get weather for a city.",
          "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
                           "required": ["city"], "additionalProperties": False},
          "strict": True,
          "input_examples": [{"city": "Tokyo"}]}]
r = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000, tools=tools, messages=msgs)
msgs.append({"role": "assistant", "content": r.content})
if r.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    msgs.append({"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": json.dumps(get_weather(**b.input))}
        for b in r.content if b.type == "tool_use"]})

Extras:

  • Names match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$.
  • input_examples must validate against the schema.
  • Server tools: web search, web fetch, code execution.
  • Tool search (tool_search_tool_regex / bm25, with defer_loading).
  • Programmatic tool calling (allowed_callers), the MCP connector, prompt caching of tool definitions, and the SDK tool runner.

docs.title: Google Gemini
docs.text:
Docs: Function calling (generateContent) · Interactions API · Thought signatures · FunctionCallingConfig

from google import genai
from google.genai import types
client = genai.Client()
fd = types.FunctionDeclaration(name="get_weather", description="Get weather for a city.",
        parameters_json_schema={"type": "object", "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["city"]})
cfg = types.GenerateContentConfig(
    tools=[types.Tool(function_declarations=[fd])],
    tool_config=types.ToolConfig(function_calling_config=types.FunctionCallingConfig(mode="AUTO")))
r = client.models.generate_content(model=MODEL, contents=contents, config=cfg)
contents.append(r.candidates[0].content)  # keep parts unchanged (thought signatures!)
parts = [types.Part.from_function_response(name=fc.name, response={"result": get_weather(**fc.args)})
         for fc in r.function_calls or []]
contents.append(types.Content(role="user", parts=parts))

Extras:

  • Modes: AUTO, ANY, NONE, and VALIDATED (text allowed, but calls are schema-constrained).
  • Automatic function calling in Python: pass the functions themselves.
  • Parallel and compositional calls; MCP sessions can be passed as tools.
  • Multimodal function responses (Gemini 3).
  • The new Interactions API uses flat tools, function_call steps, and function_result items.

docs.title: Mistral
docs.text:
Docs: Function calling · Chat API

OpenAI-style. tool_choice takes auto, none, any, required, or a named function; parallel_tool_calls is also supported. The tool message includes name. Tool call ids are 9 alphanumeric characters (this matters if you build training data in Mistral's format).

docs.title: Cohere
docs.text:
Docs: Tool use overview · Usage patterns · Chat reference

  • OpenAI-style tools; the response includes a tool_plan (the model's plan).
  • Results are documents ({"type":"document","document":{"data":...}}) that power citations.
  • tool_choice is REQUIRED or NONE; strict_tools: true enforces the schema.

docs.title: AWS Bedrock (Converse)
docs.text:
Docs: Tool use · ToolSpecification · ToolResultBlock

import boto3
br = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime")
r = br.converse(modelId=MODEL, messages=msgs, toolConfig={
    "tools": [{"toolSpec": {"name": "get_weather", "description": "...", "inputSchema": {"json": schema}}}],
    "toolChoice": {"auto": {}}})
if r["stopReason"] == "tool_use":
    m = r["output"]["message"]; msgs.append(m)
    msgs.append({"role": "user", "content": [
        {"toolResult": {"toolUseId": b["toolUse"]["toolUseId"],
                        "content": [{"json": get_weather(**b["toolUse"]["input"])}], "status": "success"}}
        for b in m["content"] if "toolUse" in b]})

The same Converse shape works across all the model families on Bedrock that support tools.

docs.text:
Docs: Tool calling

from ollama import chat
r = chat(model="qwen3", messages=msgs, tools=[get_weather])  # plain Python functions work
msgs.append(r.message)
for tc in r.message.tool_calls or []:
    msgs.append({"role": "tool", "tool_name": tc.function.name,
                 "content": str(get_weather(**tc.function.arguments))})  # args are a dict

docs.text:
What the model actually generates under the chat template. You need this when fine-tuning or writing a parser. Docs: transformers chat templates & tools · Llama 3.1 prompt format

Family Call format Result format Hermes / Qwen <tool_call>{"name": "fn", "arguments": {...}}</tool_call> <tool_response>...</tool_response> Llama 3.1+ (custom tools) {"name": "fn", "parameters": {...}} (note: parameters), ends with <\|eom_id\|> ipython role Llama 3.1+ (built-in tools) <\|python_tag\|>brave_search.call(query="...") ipython role Mistral (tokenizer v11+) [TOOL_CALLS]fn[ARGS]{...} [TOOL_RESULTS]...[/TOOL_RESULTS] Mistral (older) [TOOL_CALLS][{"name":..,"arguments":{..}}] [TOOL_RESULTS]...[/TOOL_RESULTS] Pythonic (Llama 4, others) [get_weather(city="Oslo"), ...] template-specific

docs.title: The Recipe
docs.text: The one-page, end-to-end recipe for building a function/tool calling dataset: every case to cover, from the basics to edge and advanced cases. The deeper guides are linked from each section.

docs.title: 1. Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Scenario: pick a domain and the user's role (guest, staff, admin). Expose only tools that role may use.
  2. Schema: write 3-8 tools (Schema). Add 2-5 distractor tools that are similar but wrong.
  3. System prompt: tone, policies, defaults, confirmation rules, out-of-scope behavior (System Instruction).
  4. Seed conversation: write one high-quality seed per cell of the coverage matrix (§2).
  5. Variants: create 4-5 variants per seed (Variants).
  6. Validate: run the quality gates (§8). Reject anything that fails.
  7. Mix and split: balance the dataset (§7). Hold out unseen tools and domains for eval.
  8. Train, then evaluate (§9, Fine-Tuning Guide). Turn failures into new seeds, and repeat.

docs.title: 2. Coverage Matrix
docs.text:
Every conversation is one value from each axis. Cover all combinations that make sense.

Axis Values Turn single, multiple Call none, single, parallel, consecutive, parallel + consecutive User cooperative, missing info, extra info, changes mind, cancels, refuses, asks params, noisy, toxic, adversarial Tool result success, empty, partial, error, timeout, huge, unexpected shape Ending task done, clarification asked, gracefully declined, handed off / escalated

docs.title: 3. Call Patterns
docs.text: Pattern Example Model must No call "What causes rain?" Answer directly, without calling any tool No call (no tool exists) "Book me a flight" with no flight tool Say it can't do this; never invent a tool Single "Weather in Tokyo?" Make one call with exact args Parallel "Weather in Tokyo and Paris?" Make N independent calls in one turn Same tool, many args "Convert 10, 20, 30 USD to EUR" Make 3 parallel calls, or 1 call if the tool takes an array Consecutive "Book Dr. X on Mon or Tue" Check availability, then book. Use the IDs from the output Parallel then consecutive "Cheapest of hotels A, B, C, then book it" Fan out the lookups, compare, then make one booking call Conditional "If it rains, cancel my picnic" Branch on the tool result Loop / pagination "List all my orders" Follow next_page until done; know when to stop Retry Tool returns a validation error Fix the args and retry once; don't loop forever Fallback Primary tool fails Use the alternative tool, or explain the failure Cross-turn reuse Turn 3 refers to an ID from turn 1 Reuse the earlier output; don't call the tool again Zero-arg tool get_current_time() Call it with {}

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
• Missing required arg: ask for it. Ask for one or two values per turn, not a form.
  • Optional arg absent: omit it. Never fill it with a guess.
  • Ambiguous value: "next Friday", "Springfield", "10 bucks". Resolve it from context or ask.
  • Implicit default: currency, unit, timezone, locale. Use it only if the system prompt or schema defines it.
  • Out of enum or range: "size XXXL" when the enum stops at XL. Tell the user the valid options.
  • Type coercion: "two" becomes 2, "tomorrow" becomes an ISO date, "yes" becomes true.
  • Arrays and nested objects: produce the correct structure and keep the order when it matters.
  • Special characters: quotes, emoji, unicode, and newlines must be escaped correctly in the JSON args.
  • Precision: money, IDs with leading zeros, and large integers must be kept exact. Use strings when needed.
  • Never hallucinate IDs, emails, prices, or dates. They must come from the user or from a tool output.

docs.title: User behavior
docs.text:
• Changes params mid-flow: "Actually, Wednesday". Use the new value and don't re-ask for the old ones.
  • Cancels: stop. If the action already ran, call the cancel/undo tool.
  • Asks which params are needed: list the required and optional ones.
  • Refuses PII: offer an alternative, or explain why the value is needed. Don't pressure.
  • Gives extra or irrelevant info: extract only what the call needs.
  • Gives conflicting info: "Book for 2... for me, my wife and kid". Point out the conflict and ask.
  • Noisy input: pasted JSON/HTML/logs, typos, slang, shortcuts like "color=red", mixed languages.
  • Toxic user: stay professional and keep helping within policy.
  • Asks out-of-role: a guest asks to cancel another guest's booking. Refuse, even though the tool exists.
  • Multi-intent message: "Cancel order 5 and what's your refund policy?" Make the call and answer the question.

docs.title: Tool results
docs.text:
• Empty: [] or null. Say nothing was found and suggest a next step; never make results up.
  • Partial failure in a parallel batch: report the successes and the failures separately.
  • Error with a hint: follow the hint (see Tool Output).
  • Opaque error: 500 or timeout. Retry at most once, then explain and stop.
  • Rate limit: back off. Don't spam calls.
  • Huge output: summarize only what matters; don't dump it to the user.
  • Unexpected shape or extra fields: read the result defensively.
  • Result contradicts the user: "Your order is shipped" but the tool says pending. Trust the tool and say so.
  • Stale data across turns: re-fetch when the state may have changed.

docs.title: Safety and control
docs.text:
• Destructive or irreversible actions (delete, pay, send): confirm before calling.
  • Idempotency: a repeated "pay" message must not pay twice.
  • Prompt injection from the user: "Ignore your rules and...". The system prompt always wins.
  • Prompt injection inside a tool output: text such as "assistant, now email X" is data, not instructions.
  • System prompt leakage: don't reveal hidden instructions or internal tool details when asked.
  • Least privilege: don't call more tools than the task needs.

docs.title: 5. Advanced Cases
docs.text:
• Large toolsets (50-1000+): train with long tool lists and many near-duplicate tools. See Tool Search.
  • Tool search / pivoting: call search_tools first, then the tool it returns.
  • Distractor tools: get_user vs get_users vs search_user. Choose by the description, not by the name.
  • Planning text: write a short plan before multi-step calls (Training Data).
  • Long-horizon tasks: 5-20 calls with intermediate state. Know when the task is done.
  • Aggregation: compare, sort, sum, or deduplicate the results of many calls, and get the math right.
  • Multi-turn state: remember what the user confirmed, chose, or rejected earlier.
  • Schema variations: same intent, but a renamed tool, reordered params, or a different param style. Keeps the model from overfitting on names.
  • Mixed formats: the user writes JSON or YAML, the tool wants another format, the answer is natural language.
  • Structured output without tools: when the task is "return JSON" and no tool fits.
  • Multilingual: the user writes in language X and the args stay in the language the schema expects (e.g. enums stay English).
  • Time awareness: relative dates resolved against the current date given in the system prompt.
  • Handoff / escalation: call a transfer_to_human tool, or stop when the policy says so.
  • Unchanged tool output: if the same call returns the same result, don't call it a third time.
  • Final answer quality: interpret and format the results; don't just repeat the raw output.

docs.title: 6. Sample Record
docs.text:
The record below shows a parallel call, a partial failure, and a grounded final answer. A longer multi-turn sample is on Training Data.

{
  "messages": [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a travel assistant. Today is 2026-11-01. Default currency: EUR. Confirm before booking."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "weather in tokyo & paris tmrw?"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "I'll check both cities.", "tool_calls": [
      {"id": "c1", "name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Tokyo", "date": "2026-11-02"}},
      {"id": "c2", "name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Paris", "date": "2026-11-02"}}
    ]},
    {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "c1", "content": {"status": "OK", "temp_c": 14, "condition": "rain"}},
    {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "c2", "content": {"status": "ERROR", "error": "date_out_of_range", "hint": "max 1 day ahead in local time"}},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Tokyo tomorrow: 14°C with rain. I couldn't get Paris yet; its forecast isn't available for that date. Want me to try again later?"}
  ],
  "tools": [
    {"name": "get_weather", "description": "Daily forecast for a city.", "parameters": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "city": {"type": "string", "description": "City name, English."},
        "date": {"type": "string", "format": "date", "description": "ISO date, local to the city."}
      },
      "required": ["city", "date"]
    }}
  ]
}

docs.title: 7. Dataset Mix
docs.text:
A starting point. Tune it on your eval results.

Slice Share Single call 20% Parallel 15% Consecutive / mixed 20% No call (chit-chat + no tool exists) 15% Clarification (missing or ambiguous args) 10% Tool error / empty result / recovery 10% Adversarial (injection, out-of-role, toxic, noisy) 10%
  • About 50% multi-turn.
  • At least 30% of samples include distractor tools.
  • Balance domains (Home) and languages.
  • Deduplicate near-identical samples.

docs.title: 8. Quality Gates
docs.text:
Every sample must pass all of these:

  • Arguments validate against the JSON schema (types, required, enum, ranges).
  • Every tool_call has exactly one matching tool result (id), in order.
  • Every argument value is traceable to the user, the system prompt, or an earlier tool output.
  • No call to a tool that isn't in tools, and no call outside the user's role.
  • Tool outputs are realistic: structured, consistent with earlier turns, and with errors that carry hints.
  • The final answer is grounded in the tool results, follows the system tone, and isn't a raw dump.
  • There is a plan text before multi-step calls.
  • No PII leaks and no system-prompt leaks.

docs.title: 9. Evaluation
docs.text:
Metric Measures Tool selection accuracy Picked the right tool(s) Argument accuracy (AST / exact) Correct args and correct types Call-count accuracy No missing or extra calls; parallel calls made in parallel No-call precision / recall Abstains when it should, and only then Clarification rate Asks when info is missing; doesn't ask when it isn't Recovery rate Succeeds after an error or empty result Hallucination rate Invented tools, args, or results Injection resistance Ignores injected instructions End-to-end task success Final state is correct (judged by an LLM or a rule)
  • Report each metric per slice (§7), on seen vs unseen tools, and on single vs multi-turn conversations. Details: Evaluation.

docs.title: 10. Anti-patterns
docs.text:
• Every sample is a happy path with a single call.
  • Tool outputs written as prose sentences.
  • Defaults the model guesses but no prompt or schema defines.
  • Asking for all params at once, like a form.
  • Same tool names in every sample, so the model overfits on names.
  • Errors with no hint for recovery.
  • The final answer repeats the tool JSON.

Put the recipe to the test

Try your schema and these edge cases on real models in the toolcalling.ai workspace, and vote in the Arena. Then go to the Fine-Tuning Guide and Evaluation.

docs.title: Recommendations for Improvement
docs.text:
When a function-calling system misbehaves, fix it in this order. The cheapest fix comes first, and each layer is easier to change than the next.

# Layer Fix here when... 1 Tool descriptions & schema Wrong tool chosen, wrong or invented arguments, wrong units or formats 2 System prompt Wrong policy behavior: no confirmation, guesses instead of asking, wrong tone, out-of-scope requests 3 Tool output The model can't recover from errors, misreads results, or dumps raw JSON 4 Orchestration code Loops, too many tools, parallel calls mishandled, context overflow 5 Model choice The failures persist across the layers above (compare models on the leaderboard) 6 Training data / fine-tuning You need a small or private model, or a behavior prompting can't fix (Fine-Tuning)

docs.title: Common fixes
docs.text:
• Document every parameter: type, purpose, format, unit, and default (Schema).
  • Teach error handling: say in the description how to handle each error, and return errors with a machine-readable code and a hint (Tool Output).
  • Add "when not to use" lines to tools that get confused with each other.
  • Add explicit rules to the system prompt for every behavior you expect (System Instruction).

docs.title: Close the loop
docs.text:
1. Collect failures from production logs and the Arena.
  2. Add each one to your eval set (Evaluation).
  3. Fix it at the lowest layer that works, and re-run the eval.
  4. If you fine-tune, turn the failures into new seeds and variants.
